Key Findings
  1. The two cohorts are almost perfectly separable.
    A classifier trained on any single family tells I-CONECT from 90+ subjects with AUC 0.93–1.00; 279 of 547 features (51%) have a large shift (|d| ≥ 0.8). Models trained on 90+ should not be applied to I-CONECT without adaptation. details →
  2. Most of the shift comes from one I-CONECT subgroup.
    I-CONECT conversations are either short (n=85, median 451 s) or long (n=71, median 1,495 s; 90+ median 174 s). In the language family, 82% of features fall outside the 90+ range for the long subgroup but only 3% for the short one: raw counts (LIWC categories, clauses, words) simply grow with conversation length. details →
  3. Timing and turn-taking differ in both subgroups.
    Pause ratio, long pauses, turns per minute and interruption rate are far from 90+ even in short conversations (33% of temporal features out of range for the short subgroup). This is not a length effect; it points to differences in transcription, segmentation or diarization that need checking. details →
  4. Cohen's d alone misses part of the shift.
    66 features have |d| < 0.5 but KS > 0.3: the mean barely moves while the distribution shape or spread changes. 62 of them are acoustic. Conversely, d overstates the shift of count features driven by the long subgroup. details →
  5. Ratio-based and semantic features transfer best.
    All 15 language features with |d| < 0.5 are ratios or length-corrected measures (per-clause / per-T-unit rates, MTLD). The semantic family has no feature outside the 90+ range (AUC 0.93). Length-sensitive measures such as Simple TTR and content diversity should be avoided or normalised. details →
I-CONECT Splits into Long and Short Conversations

I-CONECT conversation durations are bimodal: the short subgroup ends at about 900 s and the long subgroup starts at about 1,000 s (90+ conversations rarely exceed 530 s). Subjects are split at 900 s. Comparing each subgroup with 90+ separates shifts caused by conversation length (only the long subgroup is out of range) from shifts that hold for the whole cohort (both subgroups out of range).

Medians per group, and support overlap = share of the subgroup inside the 90+ [5th, 95th] percentile range (red < 50%).

  • Length-driven (long subgroup only): total words, LIWC counts such as Adverbs, Simple TTR, content diversity. Normalising by word count or speaking time should remove most of this shift.
  • Cohort-level (both subgroups): pause ratio and turns per minute; Assent is also high in short conversations, which suggests different transcription conventions for fillers and back-channels.
  • Short subgroup only: participant talk-time ratio (short conversations are interviewer-led: median 0.13 vs 90+ 0.52).
  • Acoustic features exist for 86 I-CONECT subjects, of whom 69 are from the long subgroup, so acoustic results mainly describe the long conversations.
How to Read This Dashboard

Metrics

MetricWhat it measuresRule of thumb
Cohen's dDifference in means, in pooled-SD units; sign = direction (positive: I-CONECT higher)|d| 0.2 / 0.5 / 0.8 = small / medium / large
KS statisticLargest gap between the two cumulative distributions; sensitive to any change in location, spread or shape0 = identical, 1 = fully separable; KS > 0.3 is a clear difference
Support overlapShare of I-CONECT subjects inside the 90+ [5th, 95th] percentile range of a feature< 50% = a 90+-trained model has to extrapolate
Domain AUCHow well an L2 logistic regression on one family's features tells I-CONECT from 90+ subjects (5-fold CV)0.5 = indistinguishable, 1.0 = perfectly separable

Reading the |d| vs KS plots

RegionMeaningAction
Low |d|, low KSDistributions matchUse as is
High |d|, high KSWhole distribution shifted or out of rangeDomain adaptation, or drop
|d| < 0.5, KS > 0.3 (grey box)Shape or spread changed while the mean stays put; d misses itQuantile transform, or drop
|d| 1.5–2.5, KS ≈ 0.45 (band)Only part of I-CONECT is shifted (the long subgroup); d overstates the shiftNormalise by length, then re-check

Data caveats

  • PCA plots and domain AUC use complete cases only (no imputation). Acoustic AUC is based on 86 of 156 I-CONECT subjects.
  • The interruption rate is 0 for every I-CONECT subject: the transcripts have no overlapping turns, so this is a pipeline artefact, not behaviour.
  • Each statistic compares one subject-level value per person (mean over that subject's recordings).

  1. Per-cohort normalisation resolves most of the shift.
    401 features had a raw KS above 0.3; after the robust z-score only 78 do. Of the 278 features with a large raw shift (|d| ≥ 0.8), 148 (53%) have the same shape in the two cohorts (CCC ≥ 0.95): for them the difference was only location and scale, which each cohort's own median and IQR remove.
  2. The language family is the exception: its shape differs.
    66 of 99 language features (67%) have CCC < 0.9, and their median KS barely moves (0.45 → 0.40). These are count features that are bimodal in I-CONECT (a short-conversation and a long-conversation subgroup); a z-score shifts and rescales both modes but cannot merge them. Only 22 language features keep the same shape, and 19 of those are ratios or length-corrected measures (per-clause and per-T-unit rates, mean lengths, MTLD and TTR variants).
  3. Temporal: scale features differ, pacing features line up.
    15 of 23 temporal features have the same shape. The 8 that do not are all size or share features (ix_n_patient_turns, pt_n_utterances, pt_total_words, pt_total_speech_sec, ix_conversation_dur_sec, ix_n_turns_total, ix_patient_talk_ratio, ix_patient_word_ratio), driven by the long-conversation subgroup. Pacing features that were far from 90+ in raw terms (pause ratio, long pauses per minute, turns per minute, response latency) have CCC ≥ 0.97, so their gap is a location shift: normalisation removes it, and any real difference in pacing between the cohorts with it.
  4. Acoustic: mostly the same shape, with one weak spot.
    307 of 420 acoustic features (73%) match. 62 do not, and 40 of those are MFCC delta statistics; the worst are the whole-recording means of the deltas (13 of 13 have CCC < 0.9), which have a long one-sided tail in I-CONECT. Acoustic scores rest on only 86 I-CONECT subjects, 69 from the long subgroup.
  5. Semantic: no feature differs.
    3 of 4 semantic features have the same shape and the other is moderate. Content diversity (0.92) is the weakest, consistent with the length effect seen in the raw view.
  6. CCC adds information that KS misses.
    The two scores mostly agree (rank correlation -0.84), but 32 features have CCC < 0.9 while KS stays below 0.15: a difference in the tails that the largest-gap KS does not see.
  7. Caveat: same shape is necessary for transfer, not sufficient.
    The scores assume each cohort is normalised with its own statistics, and say nothing about whether a feature relates to cognition in the same way. Normalising also hides scale: 58 of the 347 same-shape features still have a raw SD ratio outside 0.5–2, so a model that sees raw values would still be shifted on them.
What This View Shows

Method

  • Every feature is robust-z-scored separately within each cohort: z = (x − median) / IQR, using that cohort's own median and interquartile range. This removes the location (mean) shift and the scale difference, so what is left is the difference in distribution shape (skew, tails, bimodality).
  • Median/IQR is used instead of mean/SD because a few extreme values inflate the SD and squash the rest of the distribution, which creates spurious shape differences.
  • Shape similarity is judged mainly by the Q–Q concordance (CCC): pair the two cohorts' 5th–95th percentiles and measure how closely they follow the identity line.
  • Each plot shows the two robust-z densities (left) and the Q–Q plot (right; coloured points enter the CCC, grey points 1–4 and 96–99 do not). Points on the dashed diagonal mean identical shape.
  • Single-feature analysis only; the raw-data figures in the other tab are unchanged.

Metrics

MetricMeaningRule of thumb
Q–Q CCC (primary)Lin's concordance correlation of the two cohorts' 5th–95th percentiles. Unlike Pearson r it also penalises a slope or offset away from the diagonal≥ 0.95 same shape · 0.9–0.95 moderate · < 0.9 different
KS (robust z)KS statistic between the two robust-z samples; most sensitive to the bulk of the distribution< 0.1 similar; > 0.3 clearly different
SD ratio (raw)SD(I-CONECT) / SD(90+) before normalisation, kept because normalising hides scale differencesfar from 1 = scale difference
raw d, raw KSThe statistics before normalisation, for comparison—

Result: 347 features with CCC ≥ 0.95, 63 between 0.9 and 0.95, 136 below 0.9. CCC and KS mostly agree; when they do not, CCC usually flags a tail difference that KS (which looks at the single largest gap) misses. A similar shape after normalisation is necessary for transfer but not sufficient: it assumes each cohort is normalised with its own statistics and says nothing about whether the feature relates to cognition the same way. Skipped: ix_interruption_rate (I-CONECT: constant). IQR fallback: Swear words (90+: IQR = 0, scaled by SD).
